articles.title: Scrolling Gets Smarter with Markers, Buttons, and Scroll State
articles.body:
Scroll UI used to split neatly into two categories.

Either you left it mostly alone and accepted the browser defaults, or you built something custom and signed yourself up for a surprising amount of JavaScript.

Carousels, sticky headers, active section indicators, pagination dots, scroll-triggered effects—none of these were impossible. They just usually involved a lot of wiring.

That is what makes this moment interesting. CSS is starting to understand scroll state in a much more direct way.

Why scroll-based UI has always been awkward

A lot of front-end patterns depend on scroll state, but CSS historically had very little awareness of it.

You could make something sticky, but not easily detect when it was actually stuck. You could build a carousel, but the pagination dots and buttons usually needed JavaScript to stay in sync. You could highlight the section currently in view, but again, that usually meant observers, event listeners, and state management.

None of that was especially elegant. It worked, but it always felt like the browser knew what was happening and just was not letting CSS participate.

These newer features start to close that gap.

What is changing in modern CSS

There is not just one new feature here. It is more like a cluster of related updates that all point in the same direction.

Container scroll-state() queries let CSS react to things like whether something is stuck, snapped, or scrollable. :target-current gives you a way to style the currently active marker in a scroll marker group. And ::scroll-marker plus ::scroll-button() give scroll containers native hooks for pagination controls and previous/next buttons.

Taken together, they make scroll interfaces feel less like custom widgets and more like something the platform actually understands.

The mental model (this is the part that matters)

The easiest way to think about this is that CSS is getting three new kinds of awareness.

First, it can understand more about the state of scrolling itself. Second, it can expose built-in UI for navigating scroll containers. Third, it can tell you which “page” or section inside that scroll experience is currently active.

CSS is not just styling a scroller anymore. It is starting to understand the experience of moving through it.

That shift is what makes these features feel bigger than they first appear.

Detecting scroll behavior with @container scroll-state(...)

Scroll-state queries are probably the most conceptually important part of this group.

Regular container queries ask about size. Scroll-state queries ask about scroll-related conditions instead.

That means you can style descendants based on things like whether a sticky element is currently stuck, whether a snapped item is the one currently snapped into place, or whether a container can still scroll in a given direction. 

.section-heading {
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;
  container-type: scroll-state;
}

@container scroll-state(stuck: top) {
  .section-heading {
    box-shadow: 0 1px 0 rgb(0 0 0 / 0.12);
    background: color-mix(in oklab, white 88%, black);
  }
}

This is one of those features that feels obvious the moment you see it.

Sticky headers have existed for a while. Being able to style them differently when they are actually stuck is the missing half.

Styling the active position with :target-current

Once you have scroll markers, you need a way to know which one represents the current position.

That is where :target-current comes in. It selects the active scroll marker in a marker group—the one representing the section or “page” currently in view. 

::scroll-marker {
  inline-size: 0.75rem;
  block-size: 0.75rem;
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.2);
}

::scroll-marker:target-current {
  background: currentColor;
  transform: scale(1.15);
}

The practical payoff is immediate: active dots, active chapters, active slides, active sections in a scroller.

And because this is tied to the browser’s understanding of the scroll marker group, it is less brittle than trying to manually synchronize classes with JavaScript.

Native pagination with ::scroll-marker and ::scroll-button()

This is where things start to feel a little futuristic in the best way.

::scroll-marker gives elements generated markers that behave like anchors for their scroll targets. ::scroll-button() gives scroll containers generated buttons for directional navigation.

In plain terms: CSS can now help create the dots and buttons people expect in things like carousels and horizontally scrolling galleries. 

.carousel {
  overflow-x: auto;
  scroll-snap-type: inline mandatory;
  scroll-marker-group: after;
}

.carousel::scroll-button(left),
.carousel::scroll-button(right) {
  content: "";
  inline-size: 2.5rem;
  block-size: 2.5rem;
  border-radius: 999px;
  border: 1px solid rgb(0 0 0 / 0.14);
}

.slide::scroll-marker {
  content: "";
}

The impressive part is not just that the UI appears. It is that the browser understands what those controls are for.

This is a very different proposition from hand-building a slider and then teaching it how to behave.

Scroll-triggered animation gets more believable

This group of features also changes what “scroll-triggered animation” can mean.

Traditionally, that phrase meant JavaScript listening for intersections or scroll positions. Now there is a more CSS-native route, especially when paired with snapped states or sticky detection. 

.panel {
  container-type: scroll-state;
  transition: scale 180ms ease, opacity 180ms ease;
  opacity: 0.65;
  scale: 0.96;
}

@container scroll-state(snapped: inline) {
  .panel {
    opacity: 1;
    scale: 1;
  }
}

This is not the same thing as full scroll-driven animation timelines, but it covers a lot of the “make the active item feel active” territory in a clean way.

Sometimes you do not need continuous animation. You just need the right moment to react.

Where this becomes genuinely useful

Carousels are the obvious headline example, but this goes beyond carousels pretty quickly.

Think article navigation that highlights the section currently in view. Think horizontally scrolling card rails with native-feeling next and previous controls. Think sticky subheadings that visibly change when they lock into place. Think snapped panels that emphasize the currently focused item without any observer setup.

This is why people are excited. These are not weird demo-only tricks. They map directly to UI patterns teams have been building for years.

What to watch for

The honest version is that this is still modern-technique territory, not old dependable CSS.

Some of these features are new enough that support is uneven, and some related pieces are still clearly experimental in MDN’s documentation. That means progressive enhancement is the right mindset here.

It is also worth remembering that “native” does not automatically mean “done.” You still need to think about spacing, focus states, overflow behavior, and whether the UI actually benefits from extra controls.

Rule of thumb:
Treat these features as a way to simplify scroll UI you already need—not as a reason to invent a carousel where a plain list would have worked.

Can you use this today?

You can absolutely experiment with it today, and that is probably the right framing.

The underlying ideas are real and moving quickly, but this is still an area where support and implementation details matter. If you use these in production, do it as enhancement rather than dependency.

A simple baseline with regular scrolling, normal links, and no CSS-generated controls should still work. Then the newer behavior can layer on where supported.

Quick answers

Is this just for carousels?

No. Carousels are the flashy example, but active section indicators and sticky-state styling may end up being the more broadly useful patterns.

Do I still need JavaScript?

Sometimes, yes. But the amount of JavaScript needed for scroll-aware UI can be much smaller when the browser handles more of the relationship itself.

What is the biggest shift here?

CSS is getting closer to understanding scrolling as state—not just as movement.

Want to go deeper?

This whole cluster of features is worth watching because it says something bigger about where the platform is going.

Scroll UI used to be one of those areas where native browser behavior and custom front-end ambition never quite met in the middle. That middle is starting to exist now.

If modern CSS is getting more practical, this is exactly what that looks like.

articles.title: Understanding CSS Specificity (Without the Headaches)
articles.body:
CSS specificity has a reputation.

It is one of those things you learn early, sort of understand, and then occasionally fight with when something refuses to behave.

You add a class. It does not work. You make the selector more specific. It still does not work. Eventually you reach for !important and move on.

The problem is not that specificity is complicated—it is that it is easy to misunderstand how it actually works.

Why specificity feels unpredictable

At first glance, specificity seems simple. More specific selectors win.

The confusion comes from what “more specific” actually means.

A long selector is not necessarily more specific. A nested selector is not automatically stronger. And sometimes a single ID will beat a selector that looks far more complex.

Without a clear mental model, it starts to feel like guesswork.

What specificity actually is

Specificity is how the browser decides which CSS rule wins when multiple rules target the same element.

It is not about order. It is not about file structure. It is a scoring system.

Every selector is assigned a value based on what it contains, and the browser compares those values to determine the winner.

That value is usually represented as three numbers. 

0, 0, 0

Once you understand what those numbers represent, the system becomes much easier to reason about.

The three-part system

Specificity is made up of three components, read from left to right.

The first number represents IDs. The second represents classes, attributes, and pseudo-classes. The third represents element selectors and pseudo-elements. 

ID, CLASS, ELEMENT

Each part is counted separately. They are not combined into a single number—they are compared in order, from left to right.

That detail is what trips people up the most.

How each part is calculated

Let’s look at what contributes to each value.

IDs are the strongest contributors. Every ID selector adds one to the first number. 

#header {
  /* 1, 0, 0 */
}

Classes, attributes, and pseudo-classes all contribute to the second number. 

.card,
[type="text"],
:hover {
  /* 0, 1, 0 */
}

Element selectors and pseudo-elements contribute to the third number. 

div,
h1,
::before {
  /* 0, 0, 1 */
}

When you combine them, the counts add up within each category. 

#nav .item a {
  /* 1, 1, 1 */
}

One ID, one class, one element.

How the browser compares specificity

The browser does not add these numbers together. It compares them from left to right.

That means the first value (IDs) is the most important. If two selectors differ there, the rest does not matter.

For example: 

#nav a {
  /* 1, 0, 1 */
}

.main .link {
  /* 0, 2, 0 */
}

Even though the second selector has more classes, the first one wins—because it has an ID.

Only when the first values are equal does the browser move to the second number, and then the third.

Think of it less like math, and more like a priority system.

Where things usually go wrong

One common misunderstanding is assuming that longer selectors are stronger.

In reality, repeating element selectors does very little compared to adding a single class or ID. 

div div div {
  /* 0, 0, 3 */
}

.card {
  /* 0, 1, 0 */
}

The class selector wins, even though the first one looks more complex.

Another source of confusion is pseudo-classes. They count the same as classes, which means something like :hover can influence specificity more than expected.

These small details are where specificity starts to feel unpredictable—until you see the pattern.

Why specificity matters less—and more—today

Modern CSS gives you tools like @layer, :where(), and better component patterns that reduce the need to fight specificity.

But that does not make specificity irrelevant.

It still determines how rules interact inside a layer, inside a component, and across a codebase.

Understanding it means you can avoid problems instead of reacting to them.

The goal is not to “win” specificity—it is to control it.

What to watch for

The biggest trap is escalation. Once you start increasing specificity to fix a problem, it becomes harder to override things later.

That is how stylesheets become fragile over time.

It is also worth remembering that !important sits outside this system entirely. It overrides specificity, which is why it should be used carefully.

Rule of thumb:
Keep specificity as low as possible, and only increase it intentionally.

Quick answers

Does order ever matter?

Yes—but only when specificity is equal. In that case, the later rule wins.

Are IDs bad?

Not inherently, but they are very strong. Using them makes styles harder to override later.

What is the easiest way to manage specificity?

Keep selectors simple, use classes consistently, and rely on structure rather than escalation.

Want to go deeper?

Specificity is one of those concepts that becomes clearer the more you see it in real code. Once the three-part system clicks, it stops feeling like guesswork and starts feeling predictable.

It is not about memorizing rules—it is about understanding how the browser thinks.

articles.summary: Adapt styles based on actual styles—not just size
articles.title: Responsive Components with CSS Style Queries
articles.body:
Most responsive design decisions come down to size.

Viewport width, container width, breakpoints—everything is tied to how big something is.

But not every design decision is about size.

Sometimes you want a component to react to how it is styled. A theme change. A variation. A parent deciding something about its children.

CSS style queries are designed for that.

Why size-based thinking has limits

Container queries were a big step forward because they let components respond to their own space instead of the viewport.

But even that only solves part of the problem.

Not every variation in a component is driven by size. Sometimes the difference comes from context—like a theme, a variant, or a design decision made higher up in the component tree.

In those cases, we often fall back to extra classes, data attributes, or JavaScript just to communicate that state.

That works—but it is not especially elegant.

What CSS style queries actually do

Style queries let you apply styles based on the computed styles of an element—rather than its size.

In practice, that means a component can react to values like custom properties or other style-driven signals. 

@container style(--theme: dark) {
  .card {
    background: #111;
    color: white;
  }
}

Here, the component is not responding to width or height. It is responding to a styling decision: the value of --theme.

That is a different kind of responsiveness—one based on intent instead of dimensions.

The mental model (this is the shift)

It helps to think of style queries as “listening” to styles.

Instead of pushing classes down into components, you define values—often with custom properties—and let components respond to them. 

.container {
  container-type: style;
  --variant: compact;
}

@container style(--variant: compact) {
  .item {
    padding: 0.5rem;
  }
}

The component is not asking “how big am I?” It is asking:

“What kind of environment am I in?”

That distinction is subtle, but it changes how you structure your CSS.

Where this starts to feel useful

Theme-aware components

One of the most natural uses is theming.

Instead of scattering theme classes throughout your markup, you can define a theme at a higher level and let components adapt. 

.app {
  container-type: style;
  --theme: dark;
}

@container style(--theme: dark) {
  .card {
    background: #111;
    color: white;
  }
}

The component reacts without needing to know where the decision came from.

Component variants without extra classes

Variants often rely on modifier classes like .card--compact or .button--large.

Style queries offer another approach—one where the variation is expressed as a value rather than a class. 

.list {
  container-type: style;
  --density: compact;
}

@container style(--density: compact) {
  .item {
    gap: 0.5rem;
  }
}

This can make systems feel more flexible, especially as variations grow.

Context-driven styling

Sometimes a component needs to adapt based on where it lives.

Instead of writing deeply nested selectors, you can define context at the container level and let the component respond. 

.sidebar {
  container-type: style;
  --layout: dense;
}

@container style(--layout: dense) {
  .nav-item {
    padding: 0.25rem 0.5rem;
  }
}

The relationship becomes explicit, rather than implied through selector complexity.

How this differs from container queries

Container queries answer questions about size. Style queries answer questions about state.

They are not competing features—they are complementary.

You might use a container query to adjust layout when space changes, and a style query to adjust appearance when context changes.

One responds to dimensions. The other responds to decisions.

What to watch for

The biggest thing to keep in mind is that style queries depend on container context. You need to explicitly define a style container using container-type: style.

It is also worth remembering that this feature is still evolving. Support may be limited, and syntax or behavior could change as the spec matures.

And while this can reduce the need for extra classes, it does not eliminate the need for clear structure. Overusing style queries can make relationships harder to trace if you are not careful.

Rule of thumb:
Use style queries when a component should react to context—not just size.

Can you use this today?

This is still an experimental feature, so you should treat it as progressive enhancement.

That means building a solid baseline first, then layering style queries on top where supported.

If you are already using custom properties for theming or variants, you are in a good position to adopt this when support improves.

Quick answers

Is this a replacement for classes?

Not entirely. It is another tool—one that can reduce the need for classes in some situations.

Do I have to use custom properties?

They are the most common use case, because they are easy to query and propagate.

What is the biggest benefit?

Components can respond to context without being tightly coupled to markup structure.

Want to go deeper?

As CSS becomes more expressive, features like style queries point toward a more declarative way of building interfaces—one where components respond to signals instead of relying on rigid structure.

Size was the first step. Context is what comes next.

articles.title: Positioning UI the Native Way with Popovers and Anchors
articles.body:
Building things like tooltips, dropdowns, and menus has always felt a little… overengineered.

You show something on click or hover, then spend the rest of your time figuring out where it should go, how it should stay aligned, and what happens when the layout shifts.

That usually means JavaScript. Measurements. Repositioning logic. Edge-case fixes.

Native popovers and CSS anchor positioning change that equation. They let the browser handle the relationship between trigger and UI—so you can focus on what it should do, not how to keep it in place.

Why this has always been harder than it looks

On the surface, these UI patterns seem simple. A button opens a menu. A link shows a tooltip. A control reveals some extra options.

The complexity shows up the moment positioning enters the picture.

The UI element needs to stay aligned to its trigger, avoid overflowing the viewport, respond to resizing, and behave consistently across different layouts. And because CSS historically did not understand that relationship, JavaScript had to fill the gap.

Over time, that turns into a surprising amount of logic for something that should feel straightforward.

What native popovers give you

The popover attribute brings a built-in way to show and hide UI elements without wiring up custom JavaScript behavior.

You define an element as a popover, then trigger it from a button or control. The browser handles the toggling, focus behavior, and basic interaction patterns. 

<button popovertarget="menu">Open menu</button>

<div id="menu" popover>
  Menu content
</div>

That alone simplifies things—but the real value shows up when you start thinking about positioning.

Showing something is easy. Keeping it aligned is the hard part.

What CSS anchor positioning adds

CSS anchor positioning lets you tie one element’s position to another element—directly in CSS.

Instead of calculating offsets in JavaScript, you define a relationship: this element should sit relative to that one. 

.trigger {
  anchor-name: --menu-anchor;
}

.menu {
  position-anchor: --menu-anchor;
  top: anchor(bottom);
  left: anchor(left);
}

That reads almost like plain language: place the menu at the bottom-left of the trigger.

The browser now understands that connection and keeps it intact as the layout changes.

The mental model (how these work together)

These two features solve different parts of the same problem.

Popovers handle behavior—when something appears, how it opens and closes, how it interacts with focus.

Anchor positioning handles layout—where that thing should go, and how it stays aligned.

When you combine them, you get something that used to require a fair amount of custom logic:

a UI element that appears when needed and stays exactly where it belongs

The key shift is that the browser now understands the relationship between elements. You are not simulating it anymore.

Where this becomes immediately useful

Dropdown menus that stay attached

A classic dropdown is a perfect example. It should open from a trigger and stay aligned, even if the layout changes. 

<button class="trigger" popovertarget="menu">Menu</button>

<div id="menu" class="menu" popover>
  ...
</div>
.trigger {
  anchor-name: --menu;
}

.menu {
  position-anchor: --menu;
  top: anchor(bottom);
  left: anchor(left);
}

No measurements. No recalculations. Just a defined relationship.

Tooltips that follow their target

Tooltips are another place where positioning logic tends to grow quickly.

With anchors, the tooltip can stay tied to its element without manual adjustments. 

.tooltip {
  position-anchor: --target;
  bottom: anchor(top);
  left: anchor(center);
}

The layout stays stable even as content or viewport size changes.

Contextual UI that adapts naturally

More complex interfaces—like inline editors or contextual action menus—benefit even more from this model.

Instead of constantly recalculating positions, you define intent once and let the browser maintain it.

Less JavaScript, more intent

This is not about removing JavaScript entirely. It is about removing the parts that exist purely to work around missing layout capabilities.

Popovers replace a lot of show/hide wiring. Anchors replace a lot of positioning math.

What remains is logic that actually belongs in JavaScript—state, data, and interaction—not layout bookkeeping.

You are shifting from “calculate and correct” to “declare and let it work.”

What to watch for

These features are still relatively new, which means support and behavior can vary depending on your target environment.

It is also important to remember that anchor positioning defines relationships, not constraints. You may still need to think about how elements behave near edges or in tight spaces.

And while native popovers handle a lot for you, more complex interaction patterns may still require additional logic.

Rule of thumb:
Use popovers for behavior, anchors for positioning, and let the browser handle the connection between them.

Can you use this today?

Support is improving quickly, but this is still an area where you should be intentional about progressive enhancement.

A common approach is to build a functional baseline using traditional positioning, then enhance it with popovers and anchors where supported.

That way, the experience improves in modern browsers without breaking in older ones.

Quick answers

Do popovers replace modals?

Not exactly. They overlap in some cases, but popovers are more about lightweight, contextual UI.

Is anchor positioning only for popovers?

No. It can be used anywhere you want one element to follow another.

What is the biggest benefit?

You stop writing code to keep things aligned—and start describing how they should relate.

Want to go deeper?

These features are part of a broader shift toward more capable, declarative UI in the platform. As they mature, patterns that once required custom solutions start to feel native.

Tooltips, menus, and overlays used to be “special cases.” Now they are starting to feel like first-class citizens.

articles.title: Smoother Navigation with CSS Page Transitions
articles.body:
Most websites still jump from page to page.

You click a link, everything disappears, and a new page appears. It works—but it does not feel especially connected.

Smooth transitions between states used to be something you only saw in single-page apps, usually powered by a fair amount of JavaScript.

CSS page transitions bring that idea to the platform itself—so navigation can feel continuous instead of abrupt.

Why navigation has always felt a little disconnected

Traditional page navigation is a full reset. The old page is gone, the new page loads, and there is no visual relationship between the two.

From a technical perspective, that makes sense. From a user perspective, it can feel jarring—especially when the content is closely related.

Developers have tried to smooth that gap in different ways. Loading indicators, fade transitions, or full client-side routing.

But those approaches either feel superficial or require a shift in how the entire app is built.

What has been missing is a native way to animate between states—even across page navigations.

What CSS page transitions actually do

CSS page transitions—often referred to as the View Transitions API—let the browser capture the visual state of a page and animate it into the next state.

That state can be a route change, a DOM update, or a full page navigation.

Instead of instantly replacing one view with another, the browser creates a transition between them. 

::view-transition-old(root) {
  animation: fade-out 200ms ease;
}

::view-transition-new(root) {
  animation: fade-in 200ms ease;
}

This example is simple, but it shows the idea: you are styling the transition between two states, not just the states themselves.

That is the key difference.

The mental model (this is the important shift)

Normally, CSS styles elements that exist on the page.

With page transitions, you are styling something that exists between pages—a temporary visual layer that represents the “old” and “new” states.

The browser essentially takes snapshots of both states and gives you hooks to animate between them.

That means you are no longer trying to fake continuity. You are working with it directly.

You are not animating elements—you are animating the transition between states.

Where this starts to feel powerful

Smoother page navigation

The most immediate use case is simple navigation. Even a basic fade or slide can make transitions feel more intentional. 

::view-transition-old(root) {
  animation: fade-out 150ms ease;
}

::view-transition-new(root) {
  animation: fade-in 150ms ease;
}

Small change, but it removes the “hard cut” between pages.

Shared element transitions

Things get more interesting when elements persist across views—like images, cards, or headings.

You can assign a shared transition name and let the browser animate the element between its old and new positions. 

.card {
  view-transition-name: card;
}

Now the element does not just disappear and reappear—it moves and transforms.

This is where navigation starts to feel like a continuous experience.

State changes without a full reload

Page transitions are not limited to navigation. They can also be used for UI changes within a page—like expanding content or switching views.

The same idea applies: define the before and after, then style the transition between them.

Progressive enhancement, not a requirement

One of the nice things about this feature is that it enhances existing behavior rather than replacing it.

If transitions are not supported, navigation still works exactly as expected. You just do not get the animated layer in between.

That makes it a good candidate for progressive enhancement—something you add to improve the experience without making it fragile.

The baseline is still a working site. The transition is the upgrade.

What to watch for

The biggest shift is thinking in terms of states rather than elements. It takes a moment to get used to styling something that is not part of your normal DOM flow.

It is also easy to overdo it. Just because you can animate between every state does not mean you should. Subtle transitions tend to feel more natural and less distracting.

And while the API is powerful, more complex transitions may still require coordination with JavaScript—especially when timing or state becomes more dynamic.

Rule of thumb:
Use page transitions to reinforce continuity—not to show off animation.

Can you use this today?

Support is growing, but it is not universal yet—especially for cross-document (full page) transitions.

That makes it important to treat this as an enhancement rather than a dependency.

As support improves, this is likely to become a more common part of the platform, especially for navigation-heavy experiences.

Quick answers

Is this only for single-page apps?

No. It works especially well with them, but the goal is to bring similar capabilities to multi-page sites as well.

Do I still need JavaScript?

For simple transitions, not much. For more advanced coordination, you may still use it alongside CSS.

What is the biggest benefit?

Navigation feels connected instead of abrupt.

Want to go deeper?

As the platform evolves, features like this are starting to close the gap between traditional websites and application-like experiences.

The ability to define transitions between states—rather than just styling individual pages—is a big part of that shift.

Pages used to be separate moments. Now they can feel like part of the same flow.

articles.title: Rethinking CSS Resets for Modern CSS
articles.body:
CSS resets have been around forever.

They started as a way to neutralize browser inconsistencies—strip everything down, remove default margins, and build from a clean slate.

And for a long time, that made sense.

But modern CSS has changed. Browsers are more consistent. New layout tools exist. And the platform now gives you more control than it used to.

Which raises a simple question: do we still need to reset everything?

Why traditional resets feel a little outdated

Classic resets were built for a different era of CSS.

Back then, browser defaults varied widely. Margins, font sizes, line heights—everything could behave differently depending on where your code ran.

The solution was to remove as much as possible and start from zero.

That approach worked—but it also came with tradeoffs.

You lose useful defaults. You end up re-declaring basic behavior everywhere. And sometimes you override things that were already correct.

In modern CSS, that “reset everything” mindset can create more work than it saves.

What has changed in modern CSS

The biggest shift is that the platform has become more predictable—and more capable.

Browsers are far more consistent than they used to be, which reduces the need for aggressive normalization.

At the same time, newer features give you more targeted control over layout and behavior. You no longer need to wipe everything out just to get consistency.

Instead of resetting broadly, you can adjust more precisely.

The new mental model

A modern reset is less about removing everything and more about establishing a sensible baseline.

Instead of asking:

“How do I neutralize all browser styles?”

You start asking:

“What defaults do I actually want?”

That leads to a different kind of reset—one that keeps useful behavior and only adjusts what needs to change.

What a modern reset usually includes

Modern resets tend to focus on a few key areas rather than trying to control everything.

One common pattern is normalizing box sizing across elements so layout calculations are predictable. 

*, *::before, *::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

Another is removing default margins in places where they are more likely to cause inconsistency than help. 

body, h1, h2, h3, p {
  margin: 0;
}

From there, resets often shift toward improving defaults rather than removing them.

For example, making images behave more predictably inside layouts: 

img, picture {
  max-width: 100%;
  display: block;
}

Or ensuring form elements inherit typography so they feel consistent with the rest of the UI: 

input, button, textarea, select {
  font: inherit;
}

These are not “resets” in the traditional sense—they are small, intentional adjustments.

Modern CSS features that change the approach

Some newer CSS features reduce the need for heavy resets entirely.

Properties like color-scheme let you opt into system-level behavior for light and dark modes, instead of manually overriding everything. 

:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;
}

Layout tools like Flexbox and Grid also reduce the need for older layout hacks that resets used to account for.

And features like @layer give you a structured way to organize base styles, making resets part of a system instead of a standalone file. 

@layer reset, base, components;

@layer reset {
  /* baseline adjustments */
}

The platform is doing more for you—so you do not need to fight it as much.

A more practical approach

In most modern projects, a good reset is small, focused, and easy to understand.

It sets a baseline, then gets out of the way.

Instead of maintaining a long list of overrides, you define a few core rules that make layout and typography predictable—and rely on the browser for the rest.

This makes your CSS easier to read, easier to maintain, and less likely to introduce unexpected behavior.

What to watch for

The biggest risk with modern resets is going too far in the other direction—keeping defaults that do not match your design system.

A lighter reset does not mean no reset. It just means being intentional about what you change.

It is also worth remembering that different projects have different needs. A design system, a marketing site, and an application UI may all benefit from slightly different baseline choices.

Rule of thumb:
Keep the defaults that help you, and override the ones that do not.

Do you still need a reset?

Yes—but probably not the kind you used to use.

A modern reset is less about control and more about clarity. It defines how your project starts, without trying to account for every possible edge case.

In that sense, it becomes part of your system, not a workaround for the platform.

Quick answers

Should I use a popular reset library?

You can—but it is often worth understanding what it does and tailoring it to your needs.

Is normalize.css still relevant?

It can be, especially for broader compatibility. But modern browsers reduce the need for heavy normalization.

What is the biggest shift?

Moving from “remove everything” to “define a baseline.”

Want to go deeper?

As CSS continues to evolve, the need for aggressive resets will likely continue to shrink. The platform is becoming more consistent, and the tools for controlling layout and behavior are more precise than ever.

A reset used to be about fixing the browser. Now it is more about defining your starting point.

articles.summary: Align nested layouts without guessing, duplicating, or giving up
articles.title: When Grid Finally Lines Up with subgrid
articles.body:
CSS Grid is powerful—until you try to line things up across nested elements.

You define clean columns on a parent, everything looks great… and then a child component introduces its own grid. Suddenly things don’t align anymore.

So you duplicate column definitions. Or fudge spacing. Or accept that things are “close enough.”

subgrid is what you reach for when “close enough” stops being good enough.

Why nested grids never quite line up

Grid works beautifully when everything lives in one place. You define your columns, place your items, and the layout feels intentional.

The problem shows up when components start nesting.

A parent layout might define a clean column structure, but child components don’t automatically inherit that structure. If they need their own grid, they become independent.

That independence is usually where alignment starts to drift.

You end up redefining the same columns in multiple places, hoping they stay in sync. And even when they do, the connection between them is fragile.

It works—until something changes.

What subgrid actually does

subgrid lets a nested grid reuse the track definitions of its parent.

Instead of creating a completely new set of columns or rows, the child grid can say:

“Use the same structure that already exists above me.”

That means columns (or rows) stay aligned across component boundaries—without duplication.

The layout becomes one coordinated system instead of a collection of similar-looking grids.

The mental model (this is the part that clicks)

Think of subgrid as opting into a shared layout.

Normally, each grid defines its own tracks. With subgrid, the child gives up that control and inherits the parent’s structure instead. 

.parent {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr;
}

.child {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: subgrid;
}

Now the child is not guessing at column sizes—it is participating in the same system.

The key shift: you are no longer recreating layout—you are extending it.

Where this starts to matter

Consistent alignment across components

One of the most common use cases is aligning content across different sections that share a layout.

For example, a list of cards where each card has its own internal structure—but everything still needs to line up visually. 

.list {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 2fr 1fr;
}

.card {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: subgrid;
}

Titles, metadata, and actions all align without repeating column definitions.

Layouts that stay in sync as they evolve

Without subgrid, updating a layout often means updating it in multiple places.

With subgrid, the relationship is built in. Change the parent, and everything downstream stays aligned automatically.

That is a subtle shift—but it makes layouts much easier to maintain over time.

More intentional spacing and rhythm

Alignment is not just about columns—it is about spacing and rhythm across a page.

When nested elements share the same grid tracks, spacing feels consistent without needing to manually tune every component.

This is where layouts start to feel designed instead of assembled.

Columns, rows, or both

subgrid can apply to columns, rows, or both—depending on what you need. 

.child {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: subgrid;
  grid-template-rows: subgrid;
}

In practice, column subgrids tend to be more common, because horizontal alignment is usually where inconsistencies are most noticeable.

But row subgrids can be just as useful when vertical rhythm matters.

What to watch for

The biggest shift with subgrid is giving up some control at the child level.

That is the point—but it can feel limiting at first if you are used to defining layouts independently.

It also only works when there is a parent grid to inherit from. If the structure does not exist above, there is nothing to “subgrid” into.

And like most layout features, it does not solve everything on its own. You still need to think about how content flows and how components are structured.

Rule of thumb:
Use subgrid when alignment matters across boundaries—not just inside a single component.

Can you use this today?

Support for subgrid is strong in modern browsers, but it arrived later than core grid features, so it is worth checking your target environments.

If you need a fallback, the typical approach is to define a standalone grid for the child, knowing it will not align perfectly—but will still function. 

.child {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 2fr 1fr; /* fallback */
  grid-template-columns: subgrid;
}

That pattern keeps layouts usable while enhancing them where possible.

Quick answers

Is subgrid required to use Grid effectively?

Not at all. Grid works perfectly well without it. subgrid becomes valuable when you need alignment across nested structures.

Does this replace component-level layouts?

No—it complements them. You still define internal structure, but you can anchor it to a shared system.

When should I reach for it?

When you find yourself duplicating grid definitions just to keep things aligned.

Want to go deeper?

As layouts become more component-driven, the ability to coordinate structure across those components becomes more important.

subgrid is one of those features that does not look dramatic at first—but quietly solves a problem you have probably worked around more than once.

Once you start using it, duplicated grid definitions start to feel like a sign something could be simpler.

articles.summary: Remove awkward spacing around text without hacks or guesswork
articles.title: Cleaning Up the Edges with text-margin-trim
articles.body:
There is a specific kind of spacing issue that shows up in almost every design system.

You align text inside a container—maybe a card, maybe a button—and something feels slightly off. The text looks like it has extra space above or below it, even though your margins and padding are technically correct.

So you tweak things. Adjust line-height. Nudge padding. Add small offsets until it “looks right.”

text-margin-trim is designed to remove that guesswork. It lets the browser trim the extra space around text so alignment actually matches what you see.

Why text never quite lines up

When you work with text in CSS, you are not just dealing with the visible letters. You are dealing with the font’s metrics—ascenders, descenders, and built-in spacing that affects how text sits inside its box.

That is why text often appears to have extra space above the first line or below the last line, even when everything is technically aligned.

This becomes especially noticeable in tighter layouts—buttons, badges, cards—where visual balance matters more than raw measurements.

And because that spacing comes from the font itself, it is not something you can reliably “fix” with margin or padding alone.

What text-margin-trim actually does

text-margin-trim lets the browser remove the extra space at the start and end of text blocks—based on the font’s metrics.

Instead of adjusting the container, it adjusts how the text itself is measured.

That means the visual edges of the text align more closely with the edges of its container. 

.label {
  text-margin-trim: block;
}

In this case, the browser trims the space above the first line and below the last line, making the text sit more cleanly within its box.

You are not changing the text—you are changing how its boundaries are interpreted.

The mental model (what is actually happening)

It helps to think of text as having invisible padding built into it.

That padding is not something you declared—it comes from the font and how line boxes are calculated.

text-margin-trim gives you a way to trim that invisible space so the text behaves more like a visually tight element. 

text-margin-trim: block;

This trims the top and bottom edges. In some cases, you may also want more granular control depending on the layout.

The key idea: you are aligning what you see, not just what the browser calculates.

Where this starts to matter

Tighter buttons and labels

Buttons are one of the most obvious places this shows up. Even when padding is balanced, the text can feel slightly off-center. 

.button {
  padding: 0.5em 1em;
  text-margin-trim: block;
}

The result feels more visually centered without needing to tweak values by eye.

Cards and UI components

In cards or panels, headings and body text often introduce small inconsistencies in vertical rhythm.

Trimming the text edges helps everything align more cleanly within the component. 

.card-title {
  text-margin-trim: block;
}

Subtle change, but it removes that “slightly off” feeling.

Consistent vertical rhythm

When multiple text elements stack together, their built-in spacing can compound in ways that are hard to predict.

Trimming those edges makes spacing more consistent and easier to control.

Block vs inline trimming

Most use cases focus on trimming in the block direction (top and bottom), but the property is designed to work with different writing modes as well.

That means the trimming adapts based on how text flows, not just traditional horizontal layouts.

In practice, you will most often reach for: 

text-margin-trim: block;

It handles the most common alignment issues without overcomplicating things.

What to watch for

This property changes how text is visually measured, which means it can affect layouts that depend on precise spacing.

It is also font-dependent. Different fonts have different metrics, so the impact may vary slightly depending on what you are using.

And because this is a newer feature, support is still evolving. It is something to use thoughtfully, especially in production environments.

Rule of thumb:
Use text-margin-trim when text feels misaligned—even though your spacing values are correct.

Can you use this today?

This is still an emerging feature, so support is limited compared to more established CSS properties.

That makes it a good candidate for progressive enhancement rather than a core dependency.

You can apply it where supported and rely on standard spacing elsewhere without breaking layouts.

Quick answers

Is this the same as adjusting line-height?

Not quite. Line-height affects spacing between lines, while text-margin-trim affects the outer edges of the text block.

Does this replace margin or padding?

No—it complements them. It handles the space that margin and padding cannot reach.

When should I use it?

When text looks slightly misaligned, even though your layout values are correct.

Want to go deeper?

As CSS continues to expose more of the underlying behavior of text and layout, features like this help bridge the gap between technical accuracy and visual intent.

Text has always carried a bit of invisible baggage. This is one of the first tools that lets you clean it up directly.

articles.summary: Keep your alignment—without risking overflow or clipped content
articles.title: When Flexbox Needs to Play It Safe
articles.body:
Flexbox is great—right up until it isn’t.

You center something vertically, everything looks perfect… and then real content shows up. Suddenly text gets clipped, buttons disappear off the edge, or something just feels “off” in a way that is hard to debug.

The safe keyword exists for exactly that moment. It gives you the alignment you want—without letting the layout push things into places they shouldn’t go.

When alignment works… until it doesn’t

A lot of flexbox layouts start with something like align-items: center or justify-content: center. It is clean, predictable, and usually looks right during development.

The problem shows up when the content changes.

Maybe the text is longer than expected. Maybe the container is smaller than you planned for. Maybe a user zooms in or switches to a different language.

Now that perfectly centered layout can start pushing content outside of its container, or compressing things in ways that hurt readability.

And at that point, the alignment you chose is technically working—but practically getting in the way.

What safe actually does

The safe keyword modifies alignment behavior in flexbox (and other layout systems) so that it only applies when it is actually safe to do so.

In other words, it tells the browser:

“Use this alignment… unless it would cause content to overflow or become inaccessible.”

If the alignment would push content out of view or create layout issues, the browser falls back to a safer alternative—usually something like flex-start.

The result is a layout that behaves the way you expect in ideal conditions, but doesn’t break down when reality shows up.

The mental model (this is the key)

It helps to think of safe as a guardrail, not a new alignment.

You are still choosing an alignment like center, flex-end, or start. The safe keyword just tells the browser not to blindly commit to that choice if it causes problems. 

align-items: safe center;
justify-content: safe center;

That reads as:

“Center this… but don’t do anything risky to make that happen.”

Once you think of it that way, it becomes much easier to decide when to use it.

Where this actually helps

Centering content that might grow

Centered layouts are one of the most common places this shows up. They look great with short content, but can become fragile when that content expands. 

.container {
  display: flex;
  align-items: safe center;
  justify-content: safe center;
}

You get the visual balance of centering—without risking clipped or awkward layouts when things get tight.

Dialogs and constrained spaces

Modals, side panels, and smaller containers are especially sensitive to alignment issues.

In these cases, forcing perfect centering can actually make the UI harder to use if content starts to overflow. 

.modal {
  display: flex;
  align-items: safe center;
}

If space allows, it centers. If not, it prioritizes keeping content visible.

Layouts that need to degrade gracefully

Not every layout needs to be perfectly centered at all times. Sometimes it just needs to not break.

That is where safe really shines—it lets you aim for a preferred layout without committing to it at the expense of usability.

A quick note on behavior (not animation)

The safe keyword does not animate anything, and it is not about motion. It is about how the browser resolves alignment decisions.

What makes it interesting is that the behavior can change depending on the situation.

A layout might be centered under normal conditions, then shift toward a safer alignment when space becomes constrained.

That shift is not a transition—it is the browser choosing a different outcome based on the constraints you gave it.

Think of it as responsive alignment logic, not visual animation.

What to watch for

The biggest thing to keep in mind is that safe does not guarantee centering—it guarantees that centering will not cause problems.

That means your layout might not always look exactly the same, especially in edge cases. This is not a bug—it is the feature doing its job.

It is also worth remembering that this only affects alignment behavior. If your layout is already overflowing for other reasons, safe will not fix that on its own.

Rule of thumb:
Use safe when you want a preferred alignment, but not at the cost of usability.

Can you use this today?

Support for alignment safety keywords like safe is solid in modern browsers, but it is still worth checking if your project targets older environments.

The good news is that it is a progressive enhancement by nature. If a browser does not understand safe, it will simply fall back to the alignment value you provided. 

.container {
  align-items: center;
  align-items: safe center;
}

That pattern ensures a sensible default while allowing safer behavior where it is supported.

Quick answers

Is safe a replacement for center?

Not exactly. It modifies how center behaves—it does not replace it.

What is the opposite of safe?

The opposite is unsafe, which tells the browser to honor the alignment even if it causes overflow or clipping.

When should I use this?

Any time you are centering or aligning content in a space that might not always be predictable.

Want to go deeper?

Alignment in modern CSS is more nuanced than it first appears, especially when you start accounting for overflow, writing modes, and different layout systems.

The safe keyword is a small part of that—but it is one of those features that quietly makes your layouts more resilient.

It is not about making things look perfect. It is about making sure they still work when they are not.

articles.summary: Blend, tint, and shade colors directly in CSS—without breaking your palette
articles.title: Smarter Color, Less Guesswork with color-mix()
articles.body:
There’s a certain kind of CSS color work that starts out innocent and gets messy fast.

You’ve got a brand color. You need a softer version for a border, a darker version for hover, maybe a tinted background that still feels related without looking identical.

So you start guessing. A little lighter. A little more transparent. Maybe a totally different hex that “looks about right.”

color-mix() is what you reach for when you want those relationships to be intentional instead of improvised.

Why this has always been more annoying than it should be

Working with color in CSS has never been hard in the basic sense. If you know the exact color you want, you can write it.

The annoying part is everything in between.

Maybe you want a version of your accent color that is 20% softer. Maybe you want text that leans toward the background color instead of sitting on top of it too harshly. Maybe you want a hover state that clearly belongs to the same palette without feeling like you just guessed and hoped for the best.

For a long time, that usually meant one of two things: precomputing colors somewhere else, or manually inventing new ones until they felt right.

Neither is ideal. One slows down the workflow. The other turns your palette into a pile of “I think this was for the badge border?”

What color-mix() actually does

color-mix() lets you blend two colors together directly in CSS.

That means you can say, in plain terms, “give me mostly this color, with a little bit of that one mixed in.”

The result is a new computed color that still feels tied to the originals, which is exactly what makes this useful. You are not pulling random values out of the air anymore. You are defining a relationship.

That relationship can be subtle, dramatic, neutralizing, tinting, shading, or just enough to make a system feel cohesive instead of patched together.

The mental model (this is the part worth remembering)

color-mix(in <color-space>, <color-1> <percentage>, <color-2> <percentage>)

Under the hood, the syntax is a little formal. In practice, the idea is simple: pick a color space, then tell the browser how much of one color and how much of another you want.

If that sounds abstract, think of it this way:

one color sets the direction, the other color nudges it 

/* Mostly brand color, slightly pulled toward white */
background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--brand) 85%, white);

/* Brand color with some black mixed in for a darker state */
background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--brand) 80%, black);

/* A quieter border that still belongs to the palette */
border-color: color-mix(in oklab, var(--brand) 35%, canvas);

If you only remember one thing, remember this: color-mix() is less about inventing colors and more about deriving them on purpose.

Where this starts to feel genuinely useful

Softer surfaces that still feel connected

A common UI problem is needing a tinted background that clearly belongs to a component without screaming for attention. 

.notice {
  background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--accent) 14%, white);
  border: 1px solid color-mix(in oklab, var(--accent) 40%, white);
}

This is the difference between “same family” and “same exact color everywhere.”

Hover states without guessing

Hover colors are one of those tiny things that get weird fast. Too dark and the component feels jumpy. Too light and nothing really changes. 

.button {
  background: var(--brand);
}

.button:hover {
  background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--brand) 82%, black);
}

You are not hunting for a second hex value here. You are defining how the original should shift.

Text and borders that calm down a little

Sometimes the raw color is just too loud for secondary UI pieces. Mixing it toward the surrounding surface gives you a quieter version without losing the connection. 

.tag {
  color: color-mix(in oklab, var(--brand) 70%, black);
  border-color: color-mix(in oklab, var(--brand) 30%, currentColor);
}

This is especially handy when you want supporting elements to feel coordinated, not copy-pasted.

Theme-aware color relationships

This gets even better when paired with custom properties. Instead of maintaining separate hard-coded values all over the place, you can derive variations from a smaller set of core colors. 

:root {
  --brand: #5b6cff;
  --surface: white;
}

.card {
  background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--brand) 8%, var(--surface));
  border-color: color-mix(in oklab, var(--brand) 24%, var(--surface));
}

Fewer disconnected color tokens. More deliberate relationships.

A quick note on transitions and motion

color-mix() is not an animation feature by itself, but it plays nicely with animated states because it produces a normal computed color value.

In other words, if you transition a property like background-color, the browser can animate between the resulting colors just like it would with any other color. 

.chip {
  background-color: color-mix(in oklab, var(--accent) 14%, white);
  transition: background-color 180ms ease;
}

.chip:hover {
  background-color: color-mix(in oklab, var(--accent) 24%, white);
}

This makes subtle state changes feel more polished, because the colors are related before the transition even begins.

What to watch for

The big thing to remember is that the color space matters. The same two colors can mix a little differently depending on how the browser is asked to interpolate them.

That is why you will often see examples using spaces like oklab or oklch. They tend to produce blends that feel more visually even, especially compared with older RGB-style mixing that can look a little dull or uneven.

It is also worth remembering that this is still mixing colors, not magically solving contrast. A pleasant blend is not automatically an accessible one. If the color is being used for text, borders, or anything with readability implications, you still need to check the final result.

And finally: just because you can derive a dozen variations from one color does not mean you should. The point is to reduce guesswork, not create an endless gradient of barely distinguishable tokens.

Rule of thumb:
Use color-mix() when you want a color to feel derived from another color—not when you already know the exact final value.

Can you use this today?

In modern CSS workflows, often yes—but this is the kind of feature you should still treat with intention.

If your audience includes older browser environments, a fallback is still a good idea. The easiest pattern is to declare a solid fallback first, then follow it with the mixed value. 

.badge {
  background: #eef1ff;
  background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--brand) 12%, white);
}

That way, the design still holds together even if the enhancement is not available.

Quick answers

How is this different from using alpha transparency?

Transparency lets the background show through. color-mix() creates an actual new color. That distinction matters when you want consistency across different surfaces.

Should I mix with white and black all the time?

Those are the most obvious use cases, but not the only ones. Mixing with your actual surface color, text color, or another token often produces more intentional results.

Is this just for design systems?

Not at all. It is useful anywhere you want your colors to feel related instead of manually improvised.

Want to go deeper?

Once this clicks, it is worth exploring CSS color spaces a little more—especially why some mixes look smoother and more natural than others. That is where color-mix() really starts to go from handy to impressive.

articles.summary: Write less CSS, control specificity, and finally select what you actually mean
articles.title: Smarter Selectors with :is(), :where(), and :has()
articles.body:
CSS selectors used to feel pretty straightforward.

Then your project grows a little. You start repeating selectors, fighting specificity, and wishing you could just say what you actually mean instead of working around what CSS allows.

That is where :is(), :where(), and :has() come in.

They are not just “new pseudo-classes.” Together, they change how you think about writing selectors in the first place.

Why selectors start to feel limiting

Most of the time, CSS selectors work exactly the way you expect. You target an element, maybe add a class or two, and move on.

The friction shows up when things get more complex.

You want to style multiple variations of the same thing, but you end up repeating selectors. You want to keep specificity low, but a small change suddenly overrides something it should not. You want to style something based on its children or surroundings, and realize CSS cannot quite express that cleanly.

None of these are huge problems on their own—but together, they add up to selectors that feel more like workarounds than intent.

What these selectors actually give you

Each of these pseudo-classes solves a slightly different problem, but they all push in the same direction: letting you write selectors that match how you think about your UI.

:is() helps you group things together without repeating yourself. :where() does the same thing, but without increasing specificity. And :has() lets you select something based on what is inside it.

On their own, each one is useful. Together, they give you much more control over how selectors behave—both in terms of readability and how they interact in the cascade.

Grouping selectors with :is()

:is() is the easiest place to start because it solves a very familiar annoyance: repeating selectors.

Without it, you might end up writing something like this: 

h1, h2, h3 {
  margin-bottom: 0.5em;
}

That works—but it does not scale well when selectors get more complex.

With :is(), you can group those options in a way that stays readable even as things grow. 

:is(h1, h2, h3) {
  margin-bottom: 0.5em;
}

The real benefit shows up when the rest of the selector is doing more work. 

.article :is(h1, h2, h3) {
  color: var(--heading);
}

Same result, but easier to extend and maintain.

One important detail: :is() takes on the specificity of the most specific selector inside it. That is usually what you want—but it is something to be aware of.

Keeping specificity under control with :where()

:where() looks almost identical to :is(), but it behaves very differently in one key way.

It always has zero specificity.

That makes it incredibly useful for writing styles that should be easy to override later. 

:where(h1, h2, h3) {
  margin-bottom: 0.5em;
}

At first glance, this looks the same as :is(). The difference is what happens when something else tries to override it.

Because :where() contributes no specificity, almost any other selector can take priority without needing tricks or escalation.

This is especially useful in things like base styles or design system layers, where you want sensible defaults without making them hard to override.

Think of :where() as “grouping, but polite about it.”

Selecting based on context with :has()

:has() is where things get interesting.

It lets you select an element based on what is inside it—or what comes after it. That might not sound dramatic at first, but it unlocks patterns that were either impossible or awkward before. 

.card:has(img) {
  padding-top: 0;
}

This reads almost like plain language: “select cards that have an image.”

You can also use it for things like form states: 

form:has(input:focus) {
  outline: 2px solid var(--accent);
}

Instead of styling the input directly, you are reacting at the parent level.

This is something CSS historically struggled with, and it changes how you think about structuring styles.

The mental model (how these fit together)

It is tempting to think of these as three separate features, but they work best when you see how they complement each other.

:is() is about reducing repetition. :where() is about controlling specificity. :has() is about expressing relationships.

Put another way:

:is() simplifies what you write
:where() simplifies how it behaves
:has() expands what is possible

Once you start combining them, selectors begin to feel less like constraints and more like a language you can actually work with.

Using them together

The real payoff comes when you combine these patterns.

For example, you might want flexible heading styles that are easy to override: 

.article :where(:is(h1, h2, h3)) {
  margin-bottom: 0.5em;
}

This keeps the selector readable while ensuring it does not create unnecessary specificity.

Or you might combine grouping with contextual logic: 

.card:has(:is(img, video)) {
  padding: 0;
}

Now the component adapts based on what it contains, without extra classes or JavaScript.

This is where selectors start to feel expressive instead of restrictive.

What to watch for

The biggest thing to keep in mind is that these features change how specificity behaves—but they do not remove it entirely.

:is() still inherits specificity from its most specific argument, and :has() can create selectors that are more powerful than you expect if you are not careful.

It is also worth remembering that :has() is doing more work under the hood. While browser support is strong, you should still be thoughtful about how often and where you use it.

Rule of thumb:
Use :is() to simplify, :where() to soften, and :has() to react.

Can you use these today?

Yes, in most modern browsers.

If you are supporting older environments, :is() and :where() are generally safer bets, while :has() may need a fallback or progressive enhancement strategy.

The good news is that these features tend to enhance code readability even when used conservatively.

Quick answers

Is :is() just a shortcut?

It is a shortcut, but also a readability improvement—especially for more complex selectors.

Why not always use :where()?

Because sometimes you do want specificity. :where() is best when you intentionally want styles to be easy to override.

Is :has() a parent selector?

It is often described that way, but it is more accurate to think of it as a relational selector. It lets you match based on context, not just hierarchy.

Want to go deeper?

These selectors are part of a broader shift in CSS toward more expressive, flexible logic. As layouts and components become more dynamic, being able to describe relationships directly in CSS becomes more valuable.

Once you start using them, you will notice how many selectors used to feel like workarounds—and how much cleaner they can be when they actually match your intent.

articles.summary: Intrinsic sizes you can calculate (and animate)
articles.title: Taking Control of Intrinsic Sizes with calc-size()
articles.body:
You’ve probably heard this before: “you can’t animate height: auto.” And for a long time… that was basically true.

calc-size() changes that. It lets you do math with intrinsic sizes like auto and fit-content—which opens the door to smoother layouts, better sizing, and yes… actually animating things that used to feel impossible.

Why this has always been a pain

Intrinsic sizes—like auto, max-content, and fit-content—are incredibly useful. They let elements size themselves based on content.

The problem is… they’ve always been a dead end when you wanted control.

  • You can’t do math with them
  • You can’t tweak them
  • You can’t animate to or from them cleanly

So we’ve all done the same dance: hard-coded heights, weird max-height hacks, or just giving up on the animation entirely.

So what does calc-size() actually do?

calc-size() is basically calc()—but for intrinsic sizes.

It lets you take something like auto or fit-content and say:

  • “Give me that… plus a little more”
  • “Give me 70% of that”
  • “Round that to something cleaner”

And importantly: the result becomes something the browser can interpolate—meaning it can animate.

That’s the real unlock here. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

The mental model (this is the part that matters)

calc-size(<basis>, <math>)

Think of it like this:

  • The first value is your starting point → usually auto, fit-content, etc.
  • The second value is what you want to do to it → using size as a reference 
/* Just make auto animatable */
width: calc-size(auto, size);

/* Add breathing room */
inline-size: calc-size(fit-content, size + 2rem);

/* Scale it */
block-size: calc-size(max-content, size * 0.5);

If you remember one thing: size just means “whatever the intrinsic size would have been.”

The “this is actually useful” part

1) Auto… but not cramped

Sometimes auto is technically correct—but visually tight. 

.card {
  block-size: calc-size(auto, size + 1.5rem);
  overflow: clip;
}

Same natural height, just with a little breathing room baked in.

2) Fit-content without fighting padding

You want something to “hug” content… but not too tightly. 

button.badge {
  inline-size: calc-size(fit-content, size + 12ch);
}

This avoids weird padding + layout interactions and keeps sizing intentional.

3) Let content decide—but not too much

.column {
  inline-size: clamp(18rem, calc-size(max-content, size), 36rem);
}

Content drives the size—but you stay in control.

4) Cleaner, more consistent layouts

.tile {
  inline-size: calc-size(fit-content, round(nearest, size, 8ch));
}

This is one of those subtle polish moves that makes layouts feel “designed” instead of accidental.

The thing everyone actually wants: animating to auto

This is where calc-size() stops being “nice” and becomes “finally.”

Because the value is now interpolatable, you can transition between fixed values and intrinsic ones.

Accordion without hacks

.accordion {
  block-size: 0;
  overflow: hidden;
  transition: block-size 350ms ease;
}

.accordion[open] {
  block-size: calc-size(auto, size + 2rem);
}

No magic numbers. No guessing heights. Just… works.

Scaling intrinsic sizes

@keyframes narrower {
  from { inline-size: fit-content; }
  to   { inline-size: calc-size(fit-content, size * 0.7); }
}

You still can’t animate between different intrinsic keywords—but you can transform one into a calculated version of itself.

Where this can trip you up

  • One intrinsic basis at a time.
    You can’t mix min-content and max-content in the same calculation.
  • This isn’t always the right tool.
    If you just want animation, interpolate-size is simpler.
  • Layout animations still cost.
    This affects layout. Don’t expect transform-level performance.
Good rule of thumb:
Use calc-size() when you need both:
• intrinsic sizing
• and control over it 
.panel { inline-size: 100%; }

@supports (width: calc-size(auto, size)) {
  .panel {
    inline-size: calc-size(fit-content, size + 4rem);
  }
}

Reality check: can you use this yet?

Not fully. This is still considered experimental.

That doesn’t mean “ignore it”—it means:

  • Use it where it enhances things
  • Don’t rely on it for core layout yet
  • Always provide a fallback

Quick answers

Is this just calc()?

Not quite. calc() can’t touch intrinsic sizes. This can.

Can I animate between intrinsic values?

No—but you can animate between an intrinsic value and a calculated version of it.

When should I reach for this?

When you catch yourself thinking: “I wish auto was just a little more controllable.”

Want to go deeper?

  • MDN docs for syntax and updates
  • Spec drafts (this is still evolving)
  • Community demos—this space is moving fast
